sources.citation: Koung, Eric. 2024. Le verbe en yambɛta : de la description à l'enseignement. Mémoire de Master, Université de Yaoundé I (FALSH). 162 pp. DICAMES hdl 20.500.12177/13388.
sources.note: No word-stress statement. Sec. 1.5 'Les marques tonales en yambeta' p. 20: two level tones H and L, every syllable bears H or L, contour tones = sequences on adjacent vowels; only H marked in orthography (after Phillips 1979:107). P. 9 uses 'accentuée'/'accent sur la première syllabe' loosely for what it itself calls a 'variation tonale' in an etymology anecdote (tɛmɛn vs tɛmɛnan) -- not a stress rule.

sources.citation: Boyd, Virginia Lee (Ginger). 2015. The phonological systems of the Mbam languages of Cameroon with a focus on vowels and vowel harmony. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden. LOT Dissertation Series 410. Utrecht: LOT. xviii+413 pp. (sec. 2.3 'Yambeta phonological overview' pp. 61-82, Nigii dialect)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.3.5 Tone (p. 80-82): 'Yambeta has a two-tone system underlyingly, high and low. Rising tones and falling tones occur only due to glide formation from syllable mergers.' Noun-root melodies H/L/HL/LH, verb-root melodies L/LH/H, grammatical tone in TAM; long vowels restricted to the first root syllable (p. 66). The words stress/accent occur nowhere in the Yambeta sections (only a Dixon & Aikhenvald definition on p. 257).
